Stay out of Excel Hell

Recently I taught an Advanced Excel training course to a company and one of the things we covered was new features added to Microsoft Excel desktop over the last few years. Below I have listed 10 features along with a website link where you can learn more about these features. I encourage each of you to research and learn about one new feature a week from the list as it will make you better in excel.
​

Analyze Data

​

The analyze data feature uses AI to analyze your data and provide recommendations. You can highlight a data set and it will provide sample suggestions and also allow you to ask questions of the data. Great way to quickly create a pivot table of your data without having to do anything but click the analyze data button.

​

Learn more: Analyze Data in Excel - Microsoft Support​

​

​

Automate Tab

The automate tab has been added to the desktop. Previously the functionality was only available on the web version of Excel. The automate tab is used to automate tasks using office scripts. This is similar to using VBA to automate tasks.

​

Learn more: Automate your tasks with the Automate tab—now in Excel for Windows and Mac - Microsoft Community Hub​

​

​

Data Types

Microsoft Excel has special data types that make it easy to collect data for certain types. On the data ribbon, four types are listed Organization, Stocks, Currencies, and Geographies in the Data Types section. The organization data types are custom data types you can create for your organization. The other three are available to everyone in Excel.

​

Learn more: Excel data types: Stocks and geography - Microsoft Support​

​

​

Image Function

The image function is a new function that allows you to import images using a URL from the web.

​

Syntax: =Image(Source,[alt_text],[sizing],[height],[width])

​

Source: This is the URL link for the image you want to import

[alt_text]: This argument allows you to provide alternative text for the image.

[height]: This argument specifies the desired height of the image in pixels.

[width]: Similar to the height argument, this specifies the desired width of the image in pixels.

​

Learn more: IMAGE function - Microsoft Support​

Import Data from Picture

Within desktop Excel, you can now import data from a picture. You load a picture into Excel, and it reads the picture and inserts the data into your Excel worksheet. This is a work in process as how well it reads the picture depends on the quality of the image.

​

Learn more: Insert data from picture - Microsoft Support​

Navigation Pane

The Navigation Pane is like a Table of Contents for your workbook. It can be found in the view menu and is under the show section called Navigation. It opens the panel on the left of your screen, and the pane allows you to easily see and search different sheets and objects within your workbook.

​

Learn more: Use the Navigation pane in Excel - Microsoft Support​

Search Drop-Down Lists

​

When you create a drop-down list via the data validation function, you can now automatically search the drop-down list. Once you start typing it will automatically bring up a filtered list based on what you have typed.

​

Learn more: How to Create Excel Searchable Drop-Down Lists for Every Row - Xelplus - Leila Gharani​

Search the Menus

Microsoft now allows you to right-click and search the menus within Excel. It is the first option available when you right-click and bring up the right-click menu bar. Just type it in what you want to search and it will bring up options.

​

Learn more: How to Quickly Search the Menus in Microsoft Office (howtogeek.com)​

​

​

Show Changes

You have the ability to show all the changes you have made in a workbook. This used to be only available on the online version of Excel but it is also available in the desktop version of Excel. You can right-click on a tab and select Show Changes from the menu. It will be the last item on the menu.

​

Learn more: Get help with Show Changes in Excel - Microsoft Support​

Business Partner's Corner

As I read the book Unreasonable Hospitality, it got me thinking of how this can apply to Finance.

As a service function, we typically get requests from our cross-functional stakeholders for financial information. How can we take this to the next level and be ‘unreasonable’ by delighting our stakeholders? Here are a few of my thoughts:

1) Be brilliant on the basics. Be proactive and follow through on your commitments and see where you can overdeliver on the basics. For example, beat your deadlines. Ensure that you check your work and do not have errors that erode trust. Brilliance on the basics is foundational!

2) Take it to the next level. Think through what you could do to overdeliver what was asked. Is there any supplementary information that would be helpful? Can you provide a thoughtful recommendation even if you were not expected to provide one? Can you visualize the data in an insightful way? Can you schedule a quick discussion to follow up and see if you hit the mark? All these things add up and are steps towards earning a seat at the table.

3) Take the initiative. Surprise your stakeholders by proactively doing some additional value-added analysis. One of my go-to approaches was to do a comprehensive competitor analysis without being asked. That always worked magic in terms of showing how committed I was to the team. It is now easier than even with Chat GPT to get a great start on this. Another example could be doing a financial situation assessment of the business. In my time at Kraft Foods, I remember doing some simple analysis that showed that several products were generating an extremely small % of revenue and profit. The Marketing VP really appreciated the insights, and it was such a pleasant surprise that the finance team took that type of initiative.

In a world where we rarely see this type of service, it is a massive opportunity for all Finance professionals to deliver at an UNREASONABLE or unexpected rate!

The FP&A Guy's Tech Tips

​

In today's age of data, I believe finance professionals would benefit from learning the basics of Structured Query Language (SQL). I first learned SQL when I worked in a Business Analyst role. Learning SQL served me very well throughout my entire career. I was often able to pull data for the finance team that we would have had to wait days if not weeks to receive because I could access the data and pull the data myself. A major benefit of learning SQL is that you can also use it in Power Query within Excel and Big Query within Google not to mention databases allow you to pull data with SQL.

​

SQL is a relatively easy language to learn, and many free tutorials exist to teach SQL. I would encourage FP&A professionals to take a free course and learn the basics. Very few FP&A professionals need to become an expert but the basics will prove beneficial.

​

Below are a few free resources to help in learning the basics of SQL.

​

Free SQL Courses

  • ​Learn SQL | Codecademy​
  • ​Intro to SQL: Querying and managing data | Khan Academy​
  • ​SQLBolt - Learn SQL - Introduction to SQL​
  • ​SQL Tutorial (w3schools.com)​
  • ​Learn Intro to SQL | Kaggle​

Ron's Recommendations

​

Unreasonable Hospitality by Will Guidara

Sometimes book titles just grab you! This fantastic book by Will Guidara did just that. Thank you to Chris Ospina for the recommendation.

The book is the story of how a restaurant called Eleven Madison Park (EMP) in New York climbed to the majestic peak of being voted as the #1 restaurant in the world in 2017 with perseverance, innovation, teamwork, and an unrelentless commitment to delivering unreasonable service!

While almost all of the restaurants in the top 50 focused on being world-class in the kitchen, EMP focused on being brilliant in the kitchen AND taking service in the dining room to a new level. They focused on delighting and surprising customers.

​
One striking example is how Will overheard a foursome of tourists who said they had visited all the top restaurants in NYC, but their only regret was that they did not try a famous New York hotdog. Will and his team did not miss opportunities like that.

He quickly ran out and got them a hotdog and had the executive chef cut it in four and dress it up. Can you imagine the look on that Michelin-star quality chef? This was all in the spirit of unreasonable hospitality. There were many examples where they spent lavishly but this was an awesome example of spending very little to delight the customer. The tourists said that getting that hot dog was their favourite part of the trip.

Will talks about many of the lessons he learned from his dad Frank Guidara who was his mentor:

• How to make people feel valued and cared for.
• Paying attention to even the smallest detail in service of the customer.
• Resilience in the face of challenges. Will’s mom was sick, and he described how his dad took care of her.

He talked about how he invested a tremendous amount of time into building a team and culture. It involved bridging the typical divide between the kitchen and the dining room as well as between the new employees and the tenured employees. Will talked about the mistakes he made and admitted to his staff. He recounted the harrowing experience of running a high-end restaurant during a deep recession and how they had to cut back to survive.

It is an amazing story and a great lesson on how to delight your customer. I extend this thinking to Finance. Imagine overdelivering versus what your cross-functional partners are asking. Imagine going all-in as a business partner and being proactive and unreasonable in our quest to be great Finance business partners. Take it to the next level! More to come on this in the business partnership corner.
